title: Bodin's Démonomanie: Leading Theorist Demands Harsh Witch Prosecution
description: Jean Bodin, the foremost political theorist of the sixteenth century and author of the influential Six Books of the Commonwealth, published De la Démonomanie des Sorciers in 1580, deploying his intellectual authority to demand vigorous prosecution of witches and the suspension of normal legal protections. Bodin argued that witchcraft was a crime against God and sovereign, that the traditional rules of evidence should be relaxed because the crime was uniquely difficult to prove, and that even torture of children and weak evidence should be accepted. He devoted substantial sections to attacking Weyer, accusing him of being in league with demons. Bodin's text — by the most prestigious theorist of state power — gave witch prosecution theoretical respectability and may have influenced the intensification of prosecutions in France.
historiographical_note: Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons gives extensive analysis of Bodin's demonological arguments, showing that Bodin integrated his witch-theory into his broader political theology of sovereignty. The Démonomanie cannot be separated from Bodin's other intellectual work: his argument that witches threatened both divine and royal authority is continuous with his political theory. This integration is precisely what Clark means by taking demonology 'seriously as ideas.'
source_method: Bodin, De la Démonomanie des Sorciers (1580); Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997); secondary scholarship on Bodin
